title: Is the Network a Tree
statement:
A network has n machines, numbered 0 to n - 1, and a list of cables edges. Each edges[i] = [a, b] is a two-way cable between machines a and b. No cable connects a machine to itself, and no pair of machines has two cables.

Return true if the network is a tree: every machine can reach every other one, and there is no loop. Otherwise return false.

examples.why: All five machines are connected and no cable is redundant.
There are n − 1 = 4 cables, which a tree needs, but 0, 1, 2 form a loop and 3, 4 are cut off. Counting cables alone is not enough.
There is no loop, but the network falls apart into two pieces. Checking only for loops is not enough either.

hints: A tree has two properties. Example 2 has one but not the other, and example 3 has the other but not the first. What are they?
A connected network with n machines needs at least n − 1 cables, and a network with no loop has at most n − 1. What does that tell you about a tree's cable count?
Check that there are exactly n − 1 cables, then run one BFS from machine 0. If it reaches all n machines, it is a tree.

explain.intuition:
A tree is connected and has no loop. Both checks are needed, and the examples break each one in turn. There is a useful fact that ties them together: a tree with n nodes always has exactly n − 1 edges. Each cable you add to a connected network either joins two pieces (and there are only n − 1 joins possible before everything is one piece) or closes a loop.

So: if the cable count is not n − 1, the answer is false. If it is n − 1, the network is a tree if and only if it is connected, because a connected network with n − 1 edges cannot have a loop. One BFS from machine 0 checks connectivity. Without the counting fact, you can detect a loop directly with a DFS that remembers each node's parent: in an undirected graph, meeting an already-seen node that is not your parent means a second route, which is a loop.
steps: Build an adjacency list with both directions of every cable.
BFS from machine 0, marking machines as seen when they are pushed.
Return whether the BFS saw all n machines.
pitfalls: Checking only the cable count (example 2) or only for loops (example 3).
Treating any already-seen neighbour as a loop in the DFS version. Every cable is stored in both directions, so you always see the machine you just came from. Skip the parent.
Recursive DFS on a 100 000-machine path. That is 100 000 nested calls, far past Python's recursion limit. Use a queue or a stack.

solutions.title: DFS that remembers each parent
solutions.idea: Walk from machine 0 with an explicit stack. Meeting a seen machine that is not your parent means a loop. At the end, every machine must have been seen.

solutions.title: Count the cables, then one BFS
solutions.idea: A tree has exactly n − 1 cables. With that many, connected means no loop, so a single BFS from machine 0 settles it.

followups: Cables arrive one at a time. After each one, report whether the network is a tree so far. Which structure makes each step nearly O(1)?
Duplicate cables between the same pair are now allowed. Which of the two solutions breaks, and how do you fix it?
